The shallow aquifer is generally weakly developed, often eroded or dissolved by groundwater circulation, and commonly contains brackish or saline water. A clay-rich layer below the shallow aquifer serves as a semi-confining unit but allows some leakage between aquifer levels. The deeper aquifer system, composed mainly of the Cibao Formation and Mucarabones Sand, yields varying amounts of groundwater, although water quality decreases east of Río Piedras due to increased salinity. Recharge occurs primarily where aquifer units crop out; however, urban development has greatly restricted recharge in the SJMA (Giusti 1978; Gómez-Gómez 1987). Groundwater Development and Use Groundwater in the SJMA was among the first to be developed in Puerto Rico’s North Coast Province. However, widespread saltwater intrusion has dramatically reduced its viability. Most wells in the area have been abandoned or destroyed, particularly in central and eastern SJMA, where intrusion is most severe. Limited groundwater use persists in the western SJMA, where reduced withdrawals have slowed saltwater encroachment. The natural groundwater flow regime has been significantly altered by urbanization, historical over-pumping, and the destruction of multi-aquifer wells. Present groundwater withdrawals are modest, estimated at less than 10 million gallons per day (Gómez-Gómez 1987; Rodríguez-Martínez 1995). In a comprehensive study of groundwater along Puerto Rico’s North Coast, including the SJMA, Anderson (1976) analyzed the region’s geology, hydrology, and water quality chemistry. One key observation was that groundwater became progressively less mineralized moving inland from the coast. Higher median concentrations of dissolved solids, hardness, and bicarbonate were found in the Aguada and Aymamón limestones, which are closest to the sea. In contrast, lower concentrations were observed in the San Sebastián and Cibao formations, located farther inland. Additionally, unconfined aquifers near the coast, particularly in the SJMA, were identified as vulnerable to seawater intrusion, with evidence or potential signs of encroachment in coastal areas (Figure 7). 12 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Source: modified from Anderson (1976) 2.2 Geothermal Conceptual Model This section examines the subsurface conditions of the SJMA by developing a 3D geologic model alongside a geothermal conceptual model, utilizing a broad range of published data and literature. The 3D model was employed to evaluate potential geothermal cooling scenarios for the UPR-RP campus. The modeling process began with the collection and organization of data, following methodologies established in similar regional studies (Cumming 2009). Insights from previous studies on low-temperature geothermal technologies in other regions were also considered to guide the methodology (Wilmarth et al. 2017). Open-source Geographic Information System QGIS1 was used to clean and prepare the data, which was then input into a commercial specialized 3D modeling software package, Leapfrog Geo2, to construct the initial geologic framework.
